title: worker-app config document
description: The document carried as the config blob of a worker-app OCI artifact. It describes what a build is and what it needs. Where a deployment puts it is decided elsewhere.

contentPath.description: A path inside the content layer. Relative, forward slashes, no `..` segment, because an artifact is unpacked onto somebody else's disk.

schema_version.description: Version of this document format, not of the application. The application's version is the OCI tag, mirrored into org.opencontainers.image.version.

features.description: Named extensions this artifact relies on. A deployer that does not recognise one must refuse rather than deploy a partial configuration. Present so the format can grow without every addition becoming a schema_version bump; unknown keys elsewhere are ignored, and anything that changes deploy behaviour is named here instead.

name.description: Identifies the application. A worker whose own name equals this one is deployed under it unchanged; every other worker is deployed as `<this name>-<worker name>`. The rule does not depend on how many workers the artifact ships, so adding a second one never renames the first.

runtime.description: How this build was compiled and what the code needs from the platform. A deployment cannot override these: changing them changes which APIs the code was built against.

compatibility_date.comment: The pattern is not redundant. `format` is annotation-only in draft 2020-12 unless the format-assertion vocabulary is declared, so half of the validators in use ignore it.

limits.description: A property of the code rather than of the deployment, which is why it lives here.

cache.description: The platform edge cache in front of the Worker. A property of the code rather than of the deployment: a response is only ever cached because the code asked for it, and code that never calls the Cache API is unaffected by the switch being on. Both members are tri-state — omitting one leaves the platform's own value alone, which is not the same statement as writing false. `cross_version_cache` is the dangerous half: with it off the worker version is part of the cache key, so a deploy starts cold and can never serve a response produced by earlier code.

resources.description: Everything the code binds to. The build says which bindings exist and what kind each is; the deployment says which concrete database or bucket sits behind them.

binding.description: The name the code reads off the environment.

optional.description: The code runs without it, so a deployment may leave it unbound.

rebuildable.description: Losing the contents costs time and nothing else. Declared so a deployment can decide whether to guard against replacement, rather than guessing from the kind.

allOf.comment: A kind with no branch of its own would otherwise be completely unconstrained, since additionalProperties only consults the properties in its own schema object.

produces.description: This app writes to the queue. A queue it only consumes from, filled by something else, sets this false.

run_worker_first.description: true, false, or path globs the Worker sees before the static handler does.

allOf.comment: Kinds carrying nothing beyond the common fields. ai, browser, version_metadata and images need no deployment input at all: the binding name is the whole declaration and the platform supplies what sits behind it.

vars.description: Plain configuration the code reads. Values belong to the deployment, so only the names are here. A var the code reads and the deployment does not set is undefined at runtime, which is why declaring it earns the line.

type.description: `json` uploads the value as a JSON binding, which is how a var carries an object or a list.

default.description: A build-time fallback, not a deployment value. An explicit value from the deployment always wins.

secrets.description: Credentials the code reads. Values never appear in an artifact.

generate.description: The deployment may create this rather than being given it. For values whose only property is being unguessable and stable, where losing one costs live sessions and nothing else. A deployment keeps the value it created; changing `bytes` in a later artifact does not rotate an existing one.

one_of.description: Alternative names satisfying the same requirement. Supplying `name` OR any one of these is enough, and the worker sees whichever were supplied. One credential in two shapes is a real state during a migration, and demanding both would make the migration impossible.

workers.description: The scripts this artifact deploys. Several sharing one database and one release are one application, and splitting them across artifacts would let them drift apart.

name.description: A worker whose name equals the app name takes the deployment's script name unchanged. Every other worker is deployed as `<script name>-<name>`. The rule does not depend on how many workers the artifact ships, so adding a second one never renames the first.

main.description: Entry module, relative to the content layer root. Already bundled: nothing rebuilds it at deploy time.

modules.description: Everything besides the entry module the script needs uploaded: WebAssembly, text and data blobs, and the `_headers` and `_redirects` files, which Cloudflare takes as modules rather than as files in the assets directory. Chunks emitted next to the entry module are picked up without being listed.

content_type.description: Inferred from the extension when absent.

bindings.description: Which of the resources above this script binds. Omitted means all of them; an empty list means none.

consumes.description: Queues this script is a consumer of, as opposed to only producing to. A bare string binds with the platform defaults.

dead_letter.description: Failures go to a second queue, which the deployment names. Declared per consumer rather than per queue, because two scripts reading one queue can legitimately differ.

crons.description: Cron expressions this script's scheduled handler answers on.

routable.description: Whether a deployment may put a hostname in front of this script. A consumer-only worker sets this false, so a stray domain is a validation error rather than a live endpoint nobody meant to publish.

migrations.description: Forward-only SQL shipped with the build. This declares that the artifact carries a schema and which database it belongs to; applying it is the bootstrap endpoint's job, since the Worker already holds the binding and the alternative is a database credential on whichever machine ran the deploy.

bootstrap.description:
Installation work the artifact declares, in the order it must happen. Empty for most artifacts: three of the four applications this format was extracted from need none.

A STEP IS A DECLARATION AND NOT A PROMISE THAT ANYTHING RUNS IT. A deployer chooses which kinds it supports, and the two kinds carry very different trust:

  `endpoint` asks the deployment to POST to a path on one of this artifact's own workers. The work happens on Cloudflare, using bindings the Worker already holds, and nothing from the artifact executes on the machine holding the credentials. Prefer it.

  `run` names a program the artifact SHIPS, to be executed by the deployer. That is the deployer running code it pulled from a registry, on the machine holding its credentials, and a deployer that is not willing to do that must refuse the artifact rather than skip the step. It exists because some installation work has no Worker to talk to yet: seeding the database a Worker is about to be deployed against, before there is a Worker.

Every step must be IDEMPOTENT. A deployment runs them on every version bump, so a step that is not safe to re-run has no safe place in an apply.

name.description: Identifies the step in a log and in an error. Unique within the list.

phase.description: `pre` runs before the new version is deployed, `post` after. A step that prepares what the new code expects is `pre`; one that checks what it produced is `post`.

worker.description: For an `endpoint` step: which of this artifact's workers serves it. Must be one a hostname can reach.

endpoint.description: Path the deployment POSTs to. THE HANDLER MUST AUTHENTICATE: the caller sends a bearer token in the `authorization` header, and an endpoint that answers without one is an open installation channel on a public hostname.

run.description: Path within the content layer of a program the deployer executes. Read the description on `bootstrap` before implementing this.

env.description: Names the deployment must supply, in the JSON request body for an `endpoint` step and in the environment for a `run` step. Values belonging to the installation rather than to the build, such as the first administrator.

secrets.description: Names from the artifact's own `secrets` that this step needs. Handed over through the environment and never an argument, so they stay out of the process list.
